approachQuestion.prompt:
Fence post positions

Two integer-coordinate endpoints A and B define a closed straight fence segment. Return the number of integer-coordinate points on the segment, including its endpoints. If A=B, count that point once.

Example 1: A=(1,1),B=(7,5) -> 3, namely (1,1),(4,3),(7,5).
Example 2: A=(2,-1),B=(2,3) -> 5.
Example 3: A=(4,4),B=(4,4) -> 1.

Constraints and assumptions: Each coordinate is an integer in [-10^9,10^9]. Return a scalar count; do not enumerate or return the points. Choose the best time bound among the offered correct methods, then the least auxiliary storage when time ties.

options.text: Find gcd(abs(dx),abs(dy)) iteratively and return that value plus one, including gcd(0,0)=0.
options.feedback: Dividing the displacement by the gcd gives the smallest integer step along the line. There are g steps and g+1 points; coincident endpoints give one.

options.text: Check every integer point in the endpoints' bounding rectangle with an exact collinearity test, counting those on the segment.
options.feedback: This can return the right result, but may inspect billions of rows and columns merely to return a scalar count. This is avoidable exhaustive enumeration.
For displacement (6,4) it returns 5 instead of 3; the primitive step depends on divisibility rather than the shorter span.
For (0,0) to (1,1) it returns 3, but only the two endpoints are lattice points on the diagonal.

feedback.reason: Reduce a lattice displacement to its primitive step and handle a zero-length segment.
details: Compute dx=abs(B.x-A.x),dy=abs(B.y-A.y). Find g=gcd(dx,dy) by iterative remainder reduction, with gcd(0,0)=0. Return g+1.

The primitive integer direction divides both coordinate differences by their gcd. There are g equal lattice steps and therefore g+1 endpoint-inclusive lattice points. Coincident endpoints give g=0 and exactly one point.

“Find gcd(abs(dx),abs(dy)) iteratively and return that value plus one, including gcd(0,0)=0.”: Dividing the displacement by the gcd gives the smallest integer step along the line. There are g steps and g+1 points; coincident endpoints give one.

“Check every integer point in the endpoints' bounding rectangle with an exact collinearity test, counting those on the segment.”: This can return the right result, but may inspect billions of rows and columns merely to return a scalar count. This is avoidable exhaustive enumeration.
“Return min(abs(dx),abs(dy))+1.”: For displacement (6,4) it returns 5 instead of 3; the primitive step depends on divisibility rather than the shorter span.
“Return abs(dx)+abs(dy)+1.”: For (0,0) to (1,1) it returns 3, but only the two endpoints are lattice points on the diagonal.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed method (primitive-displacement). Let D=max(abs(dx),abs(dy)). Choose its tightest standard worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Exact signed 64-bit integer arithmetic, casting before calculations; arithmetic and comparisons cost one unit. No arbitrary-precision operations.
Iterative method, no recursion or hashing, no input copies. Auxiliary space includes all temporary state and buffers, excluding supplied input and returned output.
Include initialization and any copying; no hidden preprocessing or cache.

options.text: O(1 + log(D + 1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space
O(1 + log(D + 1)) time, O(D + 1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: One displacement gcd determines the count without walking lattice positions.
details: Computing the displacement costs constant work. Iterative Euclidean reduction has a logarithmic worst-case number of steps in the coordinate span; consecutive Fibonacci displacements attain this. The final increment and stored words are constant.
Exact signed 64-bit integer arithmetic, casting before calculations; arithmetic and comparisons cost one unit. No arbitrary-precision operations.
Iterative method, no recursion or hashing, no input copies. Auxiliary space includes all temporary state and buffers, excluding supplied input and returned output.
“O(1 + log(D + 1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Correct for the gcd calculation and constant-size state.
“O(D + 1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: This would fit enumeration along a span, not the gcd method.
“O(1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The number of remainder operations can grow with D.
“O(1 + log(D + 1)) time, O(D + 1) auxiliary space”: No lattice points or table are materialized.
